title: Time, Love, Memory: A Great Biologist and His Quest for the Origins of Behavior
author: Jonathan Weiner
note: Source 289 has a malformed combined subtitle, The Plausibility of Life; the explicit Weiner attribution and matching title identify this work, not an extra book. Selected on Charles Jennings's qualified praise in Nature Neuroscience and reader response. Scientific biography and discovery narrative pass H3 and V3. No serious veto established: the experimental history is sound, but claims about human behavior require caution. Molecular genetics is central; T11=T12=0.
notes: Jennings finds the science mostly accurate but says the book inadequately evaluates what fly experiments establish about behavior; this limits E.
Connects physics, genetics, experimental organisms and scientific communities, with limited industrial context.
Research-question selection and experimental screens offer reusable strategies for discovering mechanisms.
Clear examples of mutation-based investigation; the bridge from genes to complex behavior remains incomplete.

D=8/10, moderate confidence from contents, Jennings and detailed reader reports. Circadian clocks, courtship and memory provide distinct experimental lessons. Scientist portraits add context but sometimes displace critical analysis.
Discovery history lasts; the 1999 account of current genetics requires historical context.
Strong scientific-method relevance, less direct industrial or computing coverage.
Accomplished science reporter, assessed by a specialist editor; reporting skill is distinct from research authority.
Benzer's changing research questions provide an accessible narrative thread.
Literate and clear, but simplified gene-for-behavior language needs qualification.

title: The Maxwellians
author: Bruce J. Hunt
note: Eligible explanatory history of scientific development, not a course or historical treatise requiring reconstruction of obsolete methods. Technical material serves the historical argument. Selected on the publisher's reproduced Nature praise and a positive but small reader sample; reception confidence is moderate. No serious veto established. British setting does not make this single-nation history: the central contribution concerns internationally influential electromagnetic theory and engineering. T11=T12=0. Historical endpoint approximated at 1900.
notes: Archival historical scholarship with specialist review support; interpretation of priority and influence remains historical judgment.
Connects mathematical reformulation, physical models, experiments, telegraphy and scientific networks.
Useful account of how unfinished theories become usable tools through criticism, notation and practical problems.
Explains interactions between models, experiments and engineering constraints rather than only listing discoveries.

D=8/10, moderate confidence from detailed contents, publisher-reproduced scholarly review and reader reports. Telegraphy, ether models, wave experiments and mathematical reformulation contribute different learning. Some model explanations demand prior physics; difficulty alone is not padding.
A mature historical subject with lasting lessons in theory development.
Relevant to science and engineering organization; familiar electromagnetic content reduces marginal benefit for a theoretical physicist.
Specialist historian with sustained scholarly attention.
Interwoven biographies support the argument; technical passages are less accessible to general readers.
Careful distinctions between Maxwell's formulation and later reconstructions.

title: Brave Genius: A Scientist, a Philosopher, and Their Daring Adventures from the French Resistance to the Nobel Prize
author: Sean B. Carroll
note: Selected on specialist praise in Nature and Jon Beckwith's PLOS Biology review, with strong reader response. This does not imply consensus: Publishers Weekly criticizes its structure. Historical scientific biography is eligible; the account describes political commitments rather than recruiting readers to a current movement, so V6 is not established. No serious veto established. French wartime and intellectual history predominates (T11=-10); war, politics and philosophy are central alongside science (T12=-10). Praise therefore does not imply high personal fit.
notes: Archival research and correspondence support the account; some claims of intellectual influence remain inferred rather than directly documented.
Connects scientific work, political institutions, occupation and intellectual culture.
Cases of scientific independence and ideological pressure have transferable value, but many events are biographical particulars.
Gene regulation receives causal explanation; political and philosophical connections are less demonstrable.

D=7/10, moderate confidence from a chapter-20 excerpt, Beckwith, Nature and Publishers Weekly. Resistance organization and genetic experiments add different knowledge. The lengthy parallel narratives create uneven yield; reviewers disagree on whether the structure earns its length.
Historical discovery and institutional pressures remain relevant.
Monod's scientific organization and discoveries fit; much wartime and philosophical content is outside the preferred center.
Research biologist with substantive archival work and informed specialist attention.
Vivid passages, but the dual-biography design produces substantial structural disagreement among reviewers.
Clear scientific explanation; broader parallels are sometimes less precise.
